pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: First, the leverage improvement is real in the lender's measure but earned through earnings, not repayment. The company reports a Credit Agreement Net Leverage Ratio of 4.9x at September 30, 2026 against 5.1x at March 31, 2026, while total debt rose from USD 2,393.0 million to USD 2,412.3 million, an increase of USD 19.3 million, and the lender-defined trailing EBITDA rose from USD 441.0 million to USD 467.8 million [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics, Calculations]. That trailing figure includes USD 132.4 million (28.3%) of annualised acquisition, divestiture and synergy adjustments, and acquisition-related items together are 66.1% of it; on company-reported adjusted EBITDA without pro forma the same debt is 7.28x gross and 6.95x net [Documentary Fact for the figures, Analyst Interpretation for the reading; CP-1 Earnings quality and definitions]. For a creditor the mechanism is that leverage tolerance depends on synergies being delivered; a shortfall of 10% in the pro forma figure would add about 0.57x to gross leverage [Analyst Interpretation, derived in CP-1].

Second, cash coverage of the debt service is thin. In the six months to September 30, 2026 adjusted EBITDA was USD 222.6 million against cash interest paid of USD 90.9 million (2.45x), net cash from operations was USD 21.1 million and free cash flow USD 4.6 million, after USD 24.3 million of cash costs related to the acquisition [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics, Interpretation]. Management's guidance for fiscal 2027 is adjusted EBITDA of USD 425 million to USD 440 million and interest expense of USD 185 million to USD 190 million, which implies interest cover of about 2.3x at the midpoints, with capital expenditure guided at USD 45 million to USD 55 million [Management Language for guidance; derived in Calculations]. The mechanism is that interest, taxes, integration costs and capital spending absorb most operating cash flow, so the planned USD 150 million paydown within twelve months needs working capital release and synergy savings that are not yet in the cash flow; debt service itself is not at risk on the figures supplied.

Third, liquidity is adequate but concentrated and structurally uncertain. Liquidity was USD 532.0 million at September 30, 2026 (cash USD 110.9 million and USD 421.1 million of revolver availability), down from USD 561.2 million, with no capacity left on the USD 60.0 million receivables facility, which is borrowed by a special-purpose subsidiary, needed a waiver of its delinquency and default ratios at September 30, 2026 and was amended on October 29, 2026 [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Liquidity by facility, Covenants and compliance; CP-1A Corrections to earlier handoffs]. The revolver maturity is stated as 2031 in the latest report and as 2028 in two earlier statements, and the covenant trigger and step-down dates for the first lien leverage test (maximum 7.75x, stepping down to 6.25x) are not supplied, so the liquidity runway and covenant headroom cannot be confirmed [Documentary Fact for the conflict, Insufficient Information for the trigger; CP-0 C1, CP-1 Covenants and compliance]. The mechanism is that one revolver supplies almost all committed undrawn liquidity; a 2028 maturity would put USD 421.1 million of availability about fifteen months out.

Fourth, the structure is back-ended but floating-rate heavy. The notes of USD 900.0 million and the term loan of USD 1,449.2 million fall due in February 2033, the receivables facility in August 2028, and the only near-term maturities are planned paydown, small amortisation and a small secured building loan; about USD 586.5 million of floating-rate principal is unhedged against interest rate swaps of USD 965.0 million that begin to mature in March 2027 [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Debt structure, Calculations]. A 100 basis point rise in base rates would cost about USD 5.9 million a year on the unhedged amount (illustrative) [Analyst Interpretation]. Refinancing risk is therefore low before 2028, while interest-rate and hedge-roll risk is a monitoring item.

Fifth, business risk is moderate and better diversified than before, but its key supports are partly unproven. The product base spans hoists, lifting and securement consumables, conveyors, power controls and actuators sold through distributors across regions with about 45% of first-half revenue from outside the U.S.; management describes consumables as safety-critical, frequently replaced products, a claim that supports revenue durability if true [Management Language for the consumables claim; CP-1A Company and operating model]. The acquired business is now 55.7% of quarterly net sales, orders and sales grew in the quarter but book-to-bill was 1.0x, and legacy sales growth was 5.3% [Documentary Fact and Management Language; CP-1A]. The mechanism is that cash flow stability depends on replacement demand and industrial activity; customer and distributor concentration and the consumables share are not disclosed, so durability is a hypothesis to monitor, not a finding.

Sixth, ownership and governance are supportive on documented actions but control sits with an investor. The CD&R Investor holds all 800,000 preferred shares, about 43% as-converted (42% in one earlier report), up to three board seats and preemptive rights; the 7% preferred dividend is accruing in kind, USD 28.6 million through September 30, 2026, and the shares rank senior to common stock [Documentary Fact; CP-1A Ownership and control, CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure]. Debt reduction from divestiture proceeds and equity funding of the deal are supportive actions; the finance chief changed on July 1, 2026 during integration [Documentary Fact; CP-1A Governance and sponsor behaviour]. The mechanism is that the preferred claim accretes ahead of common holders, could turn into a cash drain if the company pays in cash or the rate rises to 10%, and gives the investor influence over capital allocation; creditor consent rights and legal capacity are unknown without the executed documents.

runs.text: Strength 1, diversified, consumables-linked franchise (Management Language for the consumables characterisation, Documentary Fact for mix and geography). Hoists are 48% of FY2026 net sales and no other line exceeds 13%; the acquisition roughly doubled first-half revenue and added consumables and Asian and Japanese operations; the company states that consumables serve safety-critical functions and are frequently replaced [CP-1A Company and operating model]. This supports revenue visibility and margin resilience; it is not yet quantified.

Strength 2, equity beneath the debt (Documentary Fact). USD 800.0 million of preferred equity, equity-classified with a carrying value of USD 818.4 million, funded about 24% of the three main funding pieces and sits below all debt [CP-1A Transaction summary, CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure]. It adds loss-absorbing capital beneath the lenders, subject to the unknown liquidation preference and redemption terms.

Strength 3, adequate liquidity and back-ended debt maturities (Documentary Fact). Liquidity of USD 532.0 million, no committed facility expiring within twelve months on the dates used, term loan and notes due in 2033 and a small mandatory amortisation [CP-1 Liquidity by facility, Debt structure]. This gives time to execute integration. The revolver date conflict and the covenant trigger qualify it.

Strength 4, active deleveraging intent and a documented use of proceeds (Management Language for the aim, Documentary Fact for the action). The company prepaid USD 193.0 million of term loan from divestiture proceeds and says it is committed to paying down debt in the near term [CP-1A Governance and sponsor behaviour]. Total debt nonetheless rose in the first half, so the intent is not yet shown in the balance sheet.

Weakness 1, high leverage that depends on pro forma earnings (Documentary Fact for the ratios, Analyst Interpretation for dependence). Gross leverage on the lender basis is 5.16x and on reported adjusted EBITDA 7.28x; 28.3% of the lender-defined EBITDA is annualisation and synergy [CP-1 Chart data, Earnings quality and definitions]. Any synergy shortfall flows straight into leverage tolerance.

Weakness 2, thin interest cover and weak free cash flow (Documentary Fact). First-half adjusted EBITDA covered cash interest 2.45x; free cash flow was USD 4.6 million; FY2026 free cash flow was negative USD 164.1 million [CP-1 Financials and credit metrics]. Debt reduction from operations is not yet visible.

Weakness 3, floating-rate exposure and one-instrument liquidity (Documentary Fact). Unhedged floating principal of about USD 586.5 million, swaps beginning to expire in March 2027, a receivables facility that required a waiver, and a revolver supplying almost all undrawn liquidity [CP-1 Debt structure, Liquidity by facility].

Weakness 4, control, governance and information gaps (Documentary Fact and Insufficient Information). A large investor with board seats and a senior accreting claim; a recent finance chief change; open conflicts on revolver maturity, ownership percentage and deal value; executed documents, customer concentration and ratings not supplied [CP-1A Ownership and control, Conflicts, Gaps]. These limit confidence rather than prove adverse behaviour.

Weakness 5, cyclical and distributor-channel exposure with acquisition-driven reporting noise (Management Language and Documentary Fact). Demand follows industrial capacity utilisation and tariffs and raw material costs are stated pressures; reported results combine two perimeter changes and preliminary purchase accounting [CP-1A Company and operating model, CP-1 Request].

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: The transaction is the acquisition of 100% of the equity of Kito Crosby Limited from funds associated with KKR, completed on February 3, 2026 after a definitive agreement announced on February 10, 2025. Status: completed; the purchase price allocation remains preliminary and the working capital adjustment is final. Three figures describe its size and they differ: the December 2025 quarterly report describes an all-cash transaction "valued at $2,700,000,000" subject to customary adjustments and regulatory approval ([10-Q Dec25 p:9]); the annual report's allocation table totals 2,811,907 ([10-K p:88]); and the September 2026 quarterly report states the all-cash transaction value as 2,821,907, which includes a 10,000 increase for the final working capital adjustment, paid after September 30, 2026 ([10-Q Sep26 p:9]). The last two reconcile by the stated adjustment (2,811,907 plus 10,000, derived); the headline-to-consideration difference is not explained in the pack and is logged as a conflict, not reconciled. Acquired cash was 184,307 ([10-Q Sep26 p:49]).

Financing, as the notes print it, was 900,000 of 7.125% senior secured notes due February 1, 2033 (issued January 30, 2026), a 1,650,000 senior secured 2026 Term Loan B maturing February 3, 2033, a new revolving credit facility of 500,000 (a 75,000 draw at closing per the December 2025 report), and 800,000 from the sale of 800,000 Series A Cumulative Convertible Participating Preferred Shares at $1,000 per share to the CD&R Investor ([10-Q Sep26 p:10, p:27-28]; [10-Q Dec25 p:10]). Proceeds also refinanced the existing 2024 Term Loan B and paid fees and expenses ([10-Q Dec25 p:10]); fees paid for borrowing on long-term debt were 91,004 in FY2026 ([10-K p:77]). Of the three principal funding pieces (notes, term loan, preferred), debt is 2,550,000 and preferred equity 800,000, so debt is about 76% and the preferred about 24% (derived); the preferred is equity-classified. The 2024 facilities were fully replaced, with no balance on the old revolver at replacement ([10-K p:110]). The new debt issues are the notes and the term loan; the term loan was repriced by 50 basis points on September 21, 2026, and the receivables facility was amended on October 29, 2026 (see CP-1 for terms and amounts). The notes carry a 101% change of control put and optional redemption from February 1, 2029 ([10-K p:110-111]); most covenants are suspended if the notes are rated investment grade by either agency ([10-K p:113]).

The related divestiture is the sale of the U.S. power chain hoist and chain manufacturing operations (Damascus, Virginia and Lexington, Tennessee) to Star Hoist Intermediate, LLC, agreed January 14, 2026 and completed March 4, 2026, which management says the company was required to make to gain regulatory approval; it produced a pre-tax gain of about 103,306 and net cash proceeds of about 183,976, and 193,010 was applied to prepay the term loan ([10-K p:12, p:89]; [10-Q Sep26 p:28]). Transition services of up to six months were provided to the buyer ([10-K p:90]). Use of proceeds therefore combined acquisition funding, refinancing and, after closing, partial deleveraging. Subsequent events inside the cutoff are the term loan repricing, the receivables facility amendment and a planned 150,000 paydown over the next twelve months (see CP-1), the 10,000 working capital payment, and the guidance increase on November 3, 2026. Liquidity effect: total liquidity moved from 561,216 at March 31, 2026 to 531,980 at September 30, 2026 (CP-1). Pro forma information in the annual report states combined net sales of about 2,035,000 for FY2026 and a net loss of about 292,000, as if the acquisition and divestiture had occurred on April 1, 2024, and is unaudited ([10-K p:90]). The commitment papers, purchase agreement, investment agreement, indenture and credit agreement are not supplied, so conditions, termination rights, representations and indemnities cannot be assessed (Insufficient Information).

fields.value: The financial base is usable but must be read in two layers. Reported (GAAP) layer: the business more than doubled in size on the Kito Crosby close (H1 FY2027 net sales 1,070,746 against 496,967 in H1 FY2026), but it is loss-making after amortization, interest and deal costs (H1 FY2027 net loss attributable to the Company 114,262; FY2026 net loss 229,535 including a 200,000 goodwill impairment), operating cash flow is small (H1 FY2027 21,065) and FY2026 operating cash flow was negative (146,211), reflecting acquisition and divestiture related cash payments. Lender-defined layer: the Credit Agreement Trailing Twelve Month Adjusted EBITDA of 467,796 at September 30, 2026 normalises a full year of Kito Crosby, the divestiture and cost synergies, and gives a Credit Agreement Net Leverage Ratio of 4.9x. The first layer is audited or filed; the second is a management reconciliation of a defined credit agreement term and is supporting evidence only. Debt is 2,412,308 (carrying value, including finance lease and the receivables facility) at September 30, 2026, up from 2,393,007 at March 31, 2026. About 1,551,465 of principal is floating rate against 965,000 of interest rate swap notional, so roughly 586,465 is unhedged on the figures supplied. Liquidity is 531,980 with the revolver commitment (500,000) the only meaningful undrawn source. The covenant package (first lien leverage test, maximum 7.75x stepping down) looks roomy against the 4.9x total net measure on an indicative reading, but trigger, step-down dates and exact definition are not supplied, so headroom is not calculable. Confidence in the base is Medium: the filed statements are internally consistent (debt carrying value ties to principal less unamortized costs; the lender-defined EBITDA reconciles line by line), while the credit documents, discrete Q4 FY2026 statements and any ratings are absent.

fields.value: Columbus McKinnon is a century-and-a-half-old US industrial manufacturer of hoists, lifting and securement hardware, precision conveyors, digital power controls and actuators, sold mainly through distributors and crane builders. On February 3, 2026 it bought Kito Crosby Limited from funds associated with KKR in an all-cash deal, financed by a 900,000 senior secured notes issue, a 1,650,000 term loan, a revolver draw and 800,000 of Series A preferred shares sold to CD&R XII Keystone Holdings, L.P. (the CD&R Investor). To gain regulatory approval it also sold its U.S. power chain hoist and chain operations on March 4, 2026 and used the proceeds to prepay the term loan. The resulting credit profile is a larger, more consumables-weighted business that is loss-making on a reported basis, carries total debt of 2,412,308 at September 30, 2026 and 531,980 of liquidity (the same figures as the CP-1 handoff), and has a large investor with board and preemptive rights whose preferred shares accrue a 7% payment in cash or in kind ahead of common shareholders. Business risk is moderated by breadth of product, brand and geography, and by consumable-type replacement demand that management describes (Management Language); it is raised by cyclical exposure to industrial activity, the distributor channel, the integration of a business of about the same size and a short-tenured finance leadership. Ownership and governance evidence shows supportive documented actions (equity funding, use of divestiture proceeds for debt reduction, in-kind preferred dividends so far) and no documented creditor-adverse or extraction-oriented action, but the legal capacity for such actions depends on credit and indenture documents that are not supplied. Confidence is Medium: the filed business and transaction facts are well sourced, while the executed transaction, investor and financing documents and any customer concentration data are missing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The transaction is the acquisition of 100% of the equity of Kito Crosby Limited from funds associated with KKR, completed on February 3, 2026 after a definitive agreement announced on February 10, 2025. Status: completed; the purchase price allocation remains preliminary and the working capital adjustment is final. Three figures describe its size and they differ: the December 2025 quarterly report describes an all-cash transaction "valued at $2,700,000,000" subject to customary adjustments and regulatory approval ([10-Q Dec25 p:9]); the annual report's allocation table totals 2,811,907 ([10-K p:88]); and the September 2026 quarterly report states the all-cash transaction value as 2,821,907, which includes a 10,000 increase for the final working capital adjustment, paid after September 30, 2026 ([10-Q Sep26 p:9]). The last two reconcile by the stated adjustment (2,811,907 plus 10,000, derived); the headline-to-consideration difference is not explained in the pack and is logged as a conflict, not reconciled. Acquired cash was 184,307 ([10-Q Sep26 p:49]).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Financing, as the notes print it, was 900,000 of 7.125% senior secured notes due February 1, 2033 (issued January 30, 2026), a 1,650,000 senior secured 2026 Term Loan B maturing February 3, 2033, a new revolving credit facility of 500,000 (a 75,000 draw at closing per the December 2025 report), and 800,000 from the sale of 800,000 Series A Cumulative Convertible Participating Preferred Shares at $1,000 per share to the CD&R Investor ([10-Q Sep26 p:10, p:27-28]; [10-Q Dec25 p:10]). Proceeds also refinanced the existing 2024 Term Loan B and paid fees and expenses ([10-Q Dec25 p:10]); fees paid for borrowing on long-term debt were 91,004 in FY2026 ([10-K p:77]). Of the three principal funding pieces (notes, term loan, preferred), debt is 2,550,000 and preferred equity 800,000, so debt is about 76% and the preferred about 24% (derived); the preferred is equity-classified. The 2024 facilities were fully replaced, with no balance on the old revolver at replacement ([10-K p:110]). The new debt issues are the notes and the term loan; the term loan was repriced by 50 basis points on September 21, 2026, and the receivables facility was amended on October 29, 2026 (see CP-1 for terms and amounts). The notes carry a 101% change of control put and optional redemption from February 1, 2029 ([10-K p:110-111]); most covenants are suspended if the notes are rated investment grade by either agency ([10-K p:113]).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The related divestiture is the sale of the U.S. power chain hoist and chain manufacturing operations (Damascus, Virginia and Lexington, Tennessee) to Star Hoist Intermediate, LLC, agreed January 14, 2026 and completed March 4, 2026, which management says the company was required to make to gain regulatory approval; it produced a pre-tax gain of about 103,306 and net cash proceeds of about 183,976, and 193,010 was applied to prepay the term loan ([10-K p:12, p:89]; [10-Q Sep26 p:28]). Transition services of up to six months were provided to the buyer ([10-K p:90]). Use of proceeds therefore combined acquisition funding, refinancing and, after closing, partial deleveraging. Subsequent events inside the cutoff are the term loan repricing, the receivables facility amendment and a planned 150,000 paydown over the next twelve months (see CP-1), the 10,000 working capital payment, and the guidance increase on November 3, 2026. Liquidity effect: total liquidity moved from 561,216 at March 31, 2026 to 531,980 at September 30, 2026 (CP-1). Pro forma information in the annual report states combined net sales of about 2,035,000 for FY2026 and a net loss of about 292,000, as if the acquisition and divestiture had occurred on April 1, 2024, and is unaudited ([10-K p:90]). The commitment papers, purchase agreement, investment agreement, indenture and credit agreement are not supplied, so conditions, termination rights, representations and indemnities cannot be assessed (Insufficient Information).

fields.value: - Revenue durability. Evidence: consumables that "serve safety-critical functions and are characterized by frequent replacement" (Management Language, [10-K p:10]); hardware share of sales 13% versus 8% ([10-K p:11]); legacy growth of 5.3% in Q2 FY2027 ([EX Nov03 p:3]). Mechanic: replacement demand reduces dependence on new capital projects and supports visibility, but hoists and cranes remain tied to industrial capital spending, and the 1.0x book-to-bill shows no order cushion. Credit implication: supportive for debt service stability if the consumables share is as management states; the share is Not disclosed and customer concentration is Not disclosed, so durability is a hypothesis to test, not a finding. Mechanic: the claim accretes ahead of common holders and could become a cash drain if the company elects cash payment or the rate rises to 10%; board seats give influence over strategy and capital allocation. Credit implication: equity cushion beneath the debt is supportive today, but control by an investor whose interests "may be different" requires monitoring of dividends, acquisitions and financing choices; legal capacity is unknown without the documents. Counter: conflict C2 on ownership percentage (42% versus 43%).

Mechanic: reporting comparability, control-environment strain and execution load during integration. Credit implication: monitoring posture should stay elevated until two clean quarters of combined reporting and a settled purchase price allocation. Counter: conflicts C1 (revolver maturity) and C5 are open and affect the debt and deal picture.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Columbus McKinnon is a leveraged but liquid industrial manufacturer whose credit profile is acceptable only if integration of its February 2026 acquisition delivers the earnings and cash flow management has assumed. Strongest support: a diversified, consumables-linked product base, USD 800.0 million of preferred equity beneath the debt, USD 532.0 million of liquidity and lender-defined net leverage of 4.9x with back-ended term debt maturities. Weakest point: reported earnings and cash flow do not yet carry the capital structure, with first-half cash interest covered only 2.45x and free cash flow of USD 4.6 million. What decides the outcome is synergy delivery, conversion of adjusted EBITDA into cash for the planned USD 150 million paydown, and the conduct of the preferred investor.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: First, the leverage improvement is real in the lender's measure but earned through earnings, not repayment. The company reports a Credit Agreement Net Leverage Ratio of 4.9x at September 30, 2026 against 5.1x at March 31, 2026, while total debt rose from USD 2,393.0 million to USD 2,412.3 million, an increase of USD 19.3 million, and the lender-defined trailing EBITDA rose from USD 441.0 million to USD 467.8 million [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics, Calculations]. That trailing figure includes USD 132.4 million (28.3%) of annualised acquisition, divestiture and synergy adjustments, and acquisition-related items together are 66.1% of it; on company-reported adjusted EBITDA without pro forma the same debt is 7.28x gross and 6.95x net [Documentary Fact for the figures, Analyst Interpretation for the reading; CP-1 Earnings quality and definitions]. For a creditor the mechanism is that leverage tolerance depends on synergies being delivered; a shortfall of 10% in the pro forma figure would add about 0.57x to gross leverage [Analyst Interpretation, derived in CP-1].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Second, cash coverage of the debt service is thin. In the six months to September 30, 2026 adjusted EBITDA was USD 222.6 million against cash interest paid of USD 90.9 million (2.45x), net cash from operations was USD 21.1 million and free cash flow USD 4.6 million, after USD 24.3 million of cash costs related to the acquisition [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics, Interpretation]. Management's guidance for fiscal 2027 is adjusted EBITDA of USD 425 million to USD 440 million and interest expense of USD 185 million to USD 190 million, which implies interest cover of about 2.3x at the midpoints, with capital expenditure guided at USD 45 million to USD 55 million [Management Language for guidance; derived in Calculations]. The mechanism is that interest, taxes, integration costs and capital spending absorb most operating cash flow, so the planned USD 150 million paydown within twelve months needs working capital release and synergy savings that are not yet in the cash flow; debt service itself is not at risk on the figures supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Third, liquidity is adequate but concentrated and structurally uncertain. Liquidity was USD 532.0 million at September 30, 2026 (cash USD 110.9 million and USD 421.1 million of revolver availability), down from USD 561.2 million, with no capacity left on the USD 60.0 million receivables facility, which is borrowed by a special-purpose subsidiary, needed a waiver of its delinquency and default ratios at September 30, 2026 and was amended on October 29, 2026 [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Liquidity by facility, Covenants and compliance; CP-1A Corrections to earlier handoffs]. The revolver maturity is stated as 2031 in the latest report and as 2028 in two earlier statements, and the covenant trigger and step-down dates for the first lien leverage test (maximum 7.75x, stepping down to 6.25x) are not supplied, so the liquidity runway and covenant headroom cannot be confirmed [Documentary Fact for the conflict, Insufficient Information for the trigger; CP-0 C1, CP-1 Covenants and compliance]. The mechanism is that one revolver supplies almost all committed undrawn liquidity; a 2028 maturity would put USD 421.1 million of availability about fifteen months out.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fourth, the structure is back-ended but floating-rate heavy. The notes of USD 900.0 million and the term loan of USD 1,449.2 million fall due in February 2033, the receivables facility in August 2028, and the only near-term maturities are planned paydown, small amortisation and a small secured building loan; about USD 586.5 million of floating-rate principal is unhedged against interest rate swaps of USD 965.0 million that begin to mature in March 2027 [Documentary Fact; CP-1 Debt structure, Calculations]. A 100 basis point rise in base rates would cost about USD 5.9 million a year on the unhedged amount (illustrative) [Analyst Interpretation]. Refinancing risk is therefore low before 2028, while interest-rate and hedge-roll risk is a monitoring item.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fifth, business risk is moderate and better diversified than before, but its key supports are partly unproven. The product base spans hoists, lifting and securement consumables, conveyors, power controls and actuators sold through distributors across regions with about 45% of first-half revenue from outside the U.S.; management describes consumables as safety-critical, frequently replaced products, a claim that supports revenue durability if true [Management Language for the consumables claim; CP-1A Company and operating model]. The acquired business is now 55.7% of quarterly net sales, orders and sales grew in the quarter but book-to-bill was 1.0x, and legacy sales growth was 5.3% [Documentary Fact and Management Language; CP-1A]. The mechanism is that cash flow stability depends on replacement demand and industrial activity; customer and distributor concentration and the consumables share are not disclosed, so durability is a hypothesis to monitor, not a finding.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Sixth, ownership and governance are supportive on documented actions but control sits with an investor. The CD&R Investor holds all 800,000 preferred shares, about 43% as-converted (42% in one earlier report), up to three board seats and preemptive rights; the 7% preferred dividend is accruing in kind, USD 28.6 million through September 30, 2026, and the shares rank senior to common stock [Documentary Fact; CP-1A Ownership and control, CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure]. Debt reduction from divestiture proceeds and equity funding of the deal are supportive actions; the finance chief changed on July 1, 2026 during integration [Documentary Fact; CP-1A Governance and sponsor behaviour].
